WARNING - LONG READ

In a recent topic about an ancestry DNA scam, I said those are scams meant to commoditize your biology. I also offered to give advice on how to research your own family history without junk science. So here we are.

Researching your family history is not a fast endeavor. It takes patience & stamina. You won’t get instant responses like with a DNA test; you will run into dead ends. Apparently I’m limited to 10k characters for this post, sorry for the choppiness.

To get started, you are going to need a place to store/organize your family history information. The best way to do this is to use a template, the most common being a family tree. There are a lot of companies who offer family tree services/software, some free, some cost. This is a pretty good summary of the most popular ones: The Best Genealogy Software of 2017.

Once you get a place to put your info, you will need to start adding it in. Start with what you know - you. Then move back in time. Fill in only facts. Don't make guesses. That will lead you down errant paths. Facts are key.

Now, you have your family tree & you have added in your information & maybe your parents/grandparents if you know it. Now what? Time to start some research.

There are a few keys to being a successful researcher. These are:

  1. Primary sources are best; multiple primary sources lead to confirmation;
  2. Know/Learn some remedial history;
  3. Know/Learn some remedial geography;
  4. Don't make assumptions/Spelling is fluid.

(1) Primary Sources

Primary sources are first-hand documents/recordings/images, etc. - 'records' for ease of reference. Your best primary sources are census records, vital records (birth/death records, marriage licenses), courthouse records (deeds, probate records, criminal/civil case records), church records, military service records, directories, & immigration records.

There are a lot of locations that house these physical records. To find where a physical record actually is located can take some work. Fortunately for us, technology has helped. There are many websites now that actively archive/digitize primary source records & make them available to the public. Some are behind paywalls, some are free. The biggest two players in this realm are Ancestry.com & FamilySearch.org

Ancestry.com Ancestry.com

Ancestry used to be a great site when they focused solely on digital records. Unfortunately, the focus now is DNA testing & social interaction. They are now actively monetizing your biology which is sickening on so many levels. Don’t get sucked in -stay focused on records.

That being said, I think a subscription to Ancestry.com is an ok idea, but a few caveats. Buy yourself only a 6 mo/year’s subscription, & buy it as a gift subscription. That way it doesn’t auto-renew. Avoid the evergreen subscription. Get the US/Canadian/UK subscription if you are just starting out. If you are a little more advanced, go for the world subscription.

If you do subscribe to Ancestry, be ready to work. You have given yourself a finite time (6 mo/1 yr) to gather as many records as possible. Spend a little time every day gathering your records. Save them to your local drive, not to the Ancestry cloud or you will lose access once your subscription ends. This also goes for the Ancestry online family tree they offer.

Ancestry also offers hints/suggestions to people they think you may be related to. Sometimes they are helpful, but I have found they are not always correct. Use these as suggestions, but like everything else, verify what you find with other records. Multiple records lead to confirmation.

FamilySearch.org FamilySearch

FamilySearch is the most comprehensive, free genealogy site out there. No other site even comes close. Before you try Ancestry, try FamilySearch first. You may need to make an account to view records, but there is no cost & you don’t have to use your real name.

As a bit of an aside, but an important one, FamilySearch is wholly owned & funded by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints aka Mormons. I am not Mormon. However, this site is very welcoming of all people interested in family history. It is my understanding that their beliefs require they research & learn about their ancestors so they can be posthumously baptized into the Church, or something like that. Basically it means their religion requires them to do genealogy, & as part of their ‘witnessing’ they spread genealogy to the world. As far as religious dogmas go, this ain’t all that bad, especially for us family historians.

Both FamilySearch & Ancestry have many of the primary record types listed above. Start looking for those first. Census records are a good bet to start. 20th cent. census records have a lot of information in the US, Canada, UK & Ireland; maybe for other countries, too. A census record usually has the name of the head of household, the names of the household members, their ages, occupations, & where they lived. This information can be used to dig down further into the identities of each person in the census. Keep in mind that the information listed in the census may not be correct. People lie; people make mistakes. Take the information you find in the Census as a guide & seek out further verification.

Besides having a large volume of digitized records, FamilySearch also has lots of resources on how & where else to research. I recommend checking out the FamilySearch Wiki. If you are looking for something specific, that is the place to go to help you narrow things down.
FamilySearch Wiki

(2) Know/Learn some remedial history

It probably wouldn’t surprise you to learn that some people are clueless on to basic timelines. For example, if your grandfather fought in WWII, he did not also fight in the US Civil War. The math just won’t add up, ever. You need to know when basic timeline events happened. You don’t have to memorize all history, just verify what you find matches up with real time events from your ancestor’s life.

It is important to know the average life span of people in the various time periods you study. For example, in the early 20th century, the average life span of a US citizen was 61. It is little things like that that are important to know.

Average ages for life events are also good to know (getting married for the first time, having their first children, etc.). Peruse some online family trees & you’ll see them riddled with math-history mistakes – like a mother having her 1st child at age 56 or a couple marrying at age 8 (that was not a thing in the western world even in old times). Don’t make those mistakes.

(3) Know/Learn some remedial geography

Again, I don’t really want to belabor what should be obvious. Keep in mind the mass mobility of people was not possible until the 20th century. Before the advent of faster transportation, people usually stayed put.

Knowing basic geography will help you narrow things down when you are faced with multiple options. Say you found your grandfather married ‘Martha Young’ in central Iowa. You search census records in central Iowa & find 4 different Martha Youngs. First, narrow down which ones were closest to him in age then by geography. A young lady would not have moved very far, if at all, from her father’s home. Your grandfather likely knew her family in some way & that is how he met Martha. Geography helps you narrow possibilities.

(4) Don't make assumptions/Spelling is Fluid

This is an important point for those searching for common names. Just because someone had your grandfather’s name & lived in the same city he did, doesn’t mean the record you are looking at is for him. This is why having multiple primary sources is the only way to authenticate you have the right ancestor.

Spelling. Not everyone knew how to read & write, & some people didn’t even know how to spell their own name. In my family, we have an ancestor from Poland. His surname only had one ‘s’ in it. Somewhere in time, an extra ‘s’ was added. This ancestor’s baptism records from Poland, immigration records, & then marriage records in the US all had the single ‘s’. It was only when children were being born that the second ‘s’ was added. There is no documentation explaining this & anyone who may have known why is now dead.

One thing to note is that the old story of an immigrant having their name changed by immigration officials is largely untrue. Immigration officials in the US/Canada did not change people’s names. In fact, most border agents were fluent in the language of the people they were checking in. What usually happened is that the immigrant themselves changed their name, not the border agent. My Polish ancestor again is an example. In Poland he was “Wladislaw”, but when he died in the US, his death certificate said ‘Walter’.

Well, this sums up the basic basics of starting & researching your family history. I hope this was helpful. I know I have not covered everything here, but it should help you get started. I want you to have some substance behind the names you find, & learn that DNA doesn’t tell you anything.

I’m happy to answer any questions you might have. I am also open to assisting you in specific research, but keep in mind talking about your family runs the risk of you being doxed. I can tell you all day that I won’t dox you (I won’t), but it’s up to you to decide on that.
